target_customer: US Department of Defense and Department of Homeland Security buyers of counter-drone systems
problem: Small drones threaten troops and US sites, and existing interceptors are one-to-one, costly or unsafe for use on US soil.
business_model: Hardware sales of man-portable launchers and low-cost guided interceptors to government customers

founders.name: Jason Cornelius
founders.background_notes: YC page says he helped lead parts of NASA's Titan Dragonfly helicopter work and founded an international drone competition.

founders.name: Steve Messinger
founders.background_notes: Swarm robotics researcher; Applied Intuition per the YC launch post.

competitors.name: Anduril
competitors.what: Reusable autonomous interceptors such as Roadrunner and the Anvil interceptor integrated into MADIS Mk 2
competitors.traction_then: Marine Corps award of $200 million in 2024 for integration, per a market roundup

competitors.name: Cambridge Aerospace
competitors.what: Tube-launched Skyhammer and Starhammer interceptors, claimed $10K to $50K unit cost
competitors.traction_then: Public debut at DSEI in September 2025
competitors.funding_then: trackers list $36M seed in May 2025 (aggregator figure)

technical_complexity.rationale: A self-guided missile needs aerodynamics, guidance, navigation and control, propulsion and live-fire testing. The team ran four major iterations and over 30 live-fire tests in eight weeks, but performance claims remain company reported.

defensibility.rationale: Testing data, DoD relationships and manufacturing know-how help, but primes and funded startups pursue the same cost-per-kill wedge.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Primes and Anduril already fielded or funded low-cost interceptors in 2024 and 2025. No acquisition of Perseus found.

market_need_then: The company cites a 2025 White House executive order on drone dominance, cost-per-engagement problems with existing kinetic defenses, and more than 100 end-user interviews across DoD and DHS.

identity.visual_style: defense hardware focus, product names HARPE and Perseus Launcher
identity.voice_and_tone: mission driven, 'America's Golden Dome for Drones'

branding.brand_signature: The line 'America's Golden Dome for Drones'
branding.community_and_virality: Trade and defense outlets covered its tests in 2026 (Golden Shield, Falcon Peak), but no merch or fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Mythological name suits defense and the company drew multiple defense press pieces within a year, though most coverage is about tests rather than the brand.

outcome_analysis: Perseus raised a reported $6M seed within weeks of Demo Day by pairing aerospace PhD founders with a timely counter-drone need and fast live-fire iteration. It showed hardware at Fort Hood and Yuma in 2026, but no confirmed government contract was found, so the next test is converting demos into funded programs against Anduril and RTX.
notes: Seed amount differs by source: $6M (Tectonic, most outlets), $6.5M (one profile), $500K (Fundup, likely partial). Lead investor: the article calls Bow Capital the largest check and names no lead. Headquarters reported as Austin or Buda, Texas by company sources and San Francisco by an aggregator. Name origin not found. Competitor figures come from market roundups, so treat as approximate.
